spec.cue: The view is soft and wide, with the ultraviolet shown as blue, and it lights up the movement around it.

cpd.note: the bee's sharpest measured limit, about 1/230 of a person

fov.note: whole-animal field of view, from a general figure for bees

fovea.note: no sharp middle is drawn for this view

gate.note: still things are left as they are

fall.note: no measured fall of sharpness with light

glow.note: movement is given a soft glow so that its speed reads

sat.note: colour is kept as a person sees it

uvBlue.note: the blue channel stands in for ultraviolet

topoA.note: no sharper middle along the long axis

field.note: the wide field is squeezed toward its edges; the app's choice

living.note: no extra weight for living movement

sweep.note: a quick scan on the body's turns

BEE.note: UV shown as blue, blue as green, green as red; pigment peaks from the cited Apidae compilation

rows: A bee sees much less detail than a person. The best measured limit is about a quarter of a grating cycle per degree, so the view is soft everywhere.
A bee sees nearly all round itself, with a small blind patch behind and below. This view squeezes a wide field into the phone.

Bees have three kinds of colour receptor, peaking in the ultraviolet, blue and green. Phone cameras capture little ultraviolet, so the view shows it as blue, and the colours shift toward the long end of the spectrum.

The soft glow on movement, the colour of that glow, the blank sharpness shape, the squeeze of the field and the lack of depth blur are the app's own choices, since no record gives values for how a bee's movement looks on screen.

claims.how: R1 gives the highest spatial frequency resolved by honeybees as 0.26 cycles per degree, and R20 gives 0.25 for Apis mellifera, so 0.26 is the value.
R35 gives a field of view of about 300 degrees horizontally for bees; it is a general figure for bees, so the grade is g.
The BEE matrix uses peaks 346, 430 and 540 nm, taken from the Apis mellifera worker entry of the Apidae compilation (R43, R73 and R85 give 346, 430 and 540), with the false colour convention of R268.

quotes.quote: They found that the highest spatial frequency reliably resolved by the bees was 0.26 cycle deg−1, with no evidence of a difference in acuity between horizontal and vertical gratings.
Bees can see ~300° horizontally on the body plane with low spatial resolution for peripheral ommatidia
using a (bathochromic) shift to longer wavelengths, by which UV is shown as blue, blue as green, green as red and red is discarded (Verhoeven et al. 2018; Fig. 4).
